name: Messapian
confidence_why: No description of Messapic says where the word accent fell: Matzinger 2019, Marchesini 2020 and Bianconi, Capano and Sabattini 2025 have no accent section, and the only hints are indirect inferences from Italian place-name reflexes such as Brundisium > Brindisi (Katičić 1976 after Çabej 1958; Demiraj 2006 after Çabej 1974) and Ribezzo 1907's passing assumption of an unstressed medial syllable in Dazimas, so any placement would be a guess.

The Hague/Paris: Mouton, p. 186 with fn. 361 (Çabej 1958: 59). org scan (item AncientLanguagesOfTheBalkans), page header '186 ILLYRIAN'. Held Messapic descriptions checked silent: Marchesini 2020 (Palaeohispanica 20, §1.4.1), Bianconi/Capano/Sabattini 2025 (IEL 13), Matzinger 2019 TOC/preface/sample pp. 7-16, Whatmough 1927/1937, Ribezzo 1907, Devoto 1978, Mayer 1939 (KZ 66), Demiraj 2006 pp. 195-196.
catalog_locator: p. 186 (Albanian-continuity toponym discussion), sentence 'One has only to suppose an initial accentuation in Illyrian..' and fn. 361
catalog_quote: But on the main Albanian names such as Lesh, Drisht, Kunavja, Drin, Buenë, Mat, and Ishm can be derived from their ancient forms Lissus, Drivastum, Candavia, Drinus, Barbanna, Mathis, and Isamnus only by Albanian sound changes, and by no others. One has only to suppose an initial accentuation in Illyrian: Dýrrachium, Ísamnus, Drívastum (cf. Messapian Brúndisium > Bríndisi). [fn. 361] Cf. Çabej (1958: 59).

new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: and the full djvu text (the scanned textpage header '186 ILLYRIAN', fn. 361 'Cf. Çabej (1958: 59)') contain the passage as quoted; the only differences are scanned artefacts the compilers silently normalised ('Ussus' for Lissus, 'Britn-disium' for Brundisium) and the footnote folded into brackets. The surrounding section (pp. 184-187) is Katičić's discussion of Albanian continuity on Illyrian soil; the sentence 'One has only to suppose an initial accentuation in Illyrian: Dyrrachium, Isamnus, Drivastum (cf. Messapian Brundisium > Brindisi)' is an explicitly suppositional, toponym-based inference about Illyrian, with Messapic entering only as the parenthetical Brindisi example.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Hypothesis only: an accent on the word-initial syllable is supposed for Illyrian (and, by the parenthetical example, for Messapic), inferred from the modern initial stress of Bríndisi < Brundisium/Brendesion, which cannot continue the Latin (Brundísium) or Greek (Brentésion) accentuation. Ribezzo 1907 tacitly makes the same assumption when he calls the second syllable of Dazimas (< *Dazamas) 'postonica'/'atona'. No description of Messapic states an accent rule; the modern grammar (Matzinger 2019) has no accent section and Marchesini 2020 / Bianconi et al. 2025 are silent — for this epigraphic Trümmersprache the accent is effectively undescribed/unknown.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the evidence base is a single toponym (Brundisium > Bríndisi) plus Balkan-Illyrian names
new_statements.domain_note: Reconstructive inference about the (prehistoric) word accent from toponym stress and vowel weakening; not a synchronic description; script gives no accent marks.
new_statements.identity_note: Messapic is a fragmentarily attested epigraphic language (ca. 600 short inscriptions in a Greek-derived alphabet without accent notation). No source describes a living accent; anything said about accent is reconstructive inference (vowel weakening in names, the modern stress of the toponym Bríndisi < Brundisium/Brendesion). The Katičić remark concerns 'Illyrian' generally, with Messapic Brundisium as the supporting example; Glottolog treats Illyrian (illy1234) and Messapic (mess1244) as distinct.

sources.citation: Neroznak, V. P. 1990. Illirijskij jazyk (→ Messapskij jazyk). Lingvističeskij ènciklopedičeskij slovar'. Moskva.
sources.note: Short phonology (two-vowel merger, diphthongs, 10 consonants); no word on stress (ударение).

sources.citation: Whatmough, Joshua. 1937. The Foundations of Roman Italy. London: Methuen. ('7. The Messapic dialect', pp. 320-322)
sources.note: Lists the main features of Messapic (o > a, bh dh > b d, gemination before i, gen. -ihi..) with no word on accent; his remarks on initial accent elsewhere (pp. 276, 336) concern Latin/Etruscan and Sicel, not Messapic.

sources.citation: Ribezzo, Francesco. 1907. La lingua degli antichi Messapii. Napoli.
sources.note: No accent paragraph (the announced 'Schizzo d'una fonetica' never appeared); incidentally speaks of 'riduzione di e in i in sillaba postonica (cfr. Dazimas da *dazamas)' and 'indebolimento storico di a in i in sillaba atona', i.e. tacitly assumes accent on the first syllable of Dazimas, without stating a rule.

sources.citation: Bianconi, Michele, Marta Capano & Paolo Sabattini. 2025. A new assessment of Messapic vocalism: sound change, script adaptation, and synchronic phonology. Indo-European Linguistics 13: 1-40. doi:10.1163/22125892-bja10039
sources.note: 41-page study of the vowel system; the only 'stress' mentions concern PIE/Vedic paradigmatic accent of *-tor- stems; no statement about the position of the Messapic word accent, and vowel alternations (dazimas ~ dazomas etc.) are not attributed to stress.
